alt: Side view of an aircraft taking three kinds of photograph: a vertical photograph looks straight down and shows no horizon (a plan like a map), a low oblique is angled but shows only ground, and a high oblique looks almost level so the horizon appears in the picture.
caption: Figure: how the camera angle gives vertical, low oblique and high oblique aerial photographs

alt: Grid with eastings 61 to 64 and northings 45 to 49: the bridge lies 2.4 km east and 3.2 km north of the dam, so its bearing from the dam, measured clockwise from grid north, is 037°, and the bearing of the dam from the bridge (back bearing) is 217°.
caption: Figure: the bearing of the bridge from the dam is 037°; the back bearing is 217°

alt: Chipo's freehand sketch map titled My village, inside a frame with a key, showing huts, a borehole, a store and a river; it has no north arrow and no scale.
caption: Figure: Chipo's sketch map of her village (it has no north arrow and no scale)

alt: Three cross-sections of a cliff: waves cut a notch at the base, the unsupported rock above collapses, and as the cliff retreats inland a gently sloping wave-cut platform is left behind.
caption: Figure: how a wave-cut platform forms as a cliff retreats

alt: Climate graph for the fictional plateau station: rainfall bars are tall from November to March (January 190 mm) and almost nil from May to September (0 mm in July), totalling 806 mm; the temperature line stays between 13 °C in June and July and 22 °C in November, an annual range of 9 °C.
caption: Figure: a climate graph, rainfall as bars and temperature as a line, for the fictional plateau station

alt: Four contour patterns: a conical hill is concentric closed contours (1500, 1520, 1540 m round a 1568 m summit); in a valley the contour Vs point uphill with the river along them; in a spur the Vs point downhill; a col is the low saddle on the 1520 m contour between two summits.
caption: Figure: contour patterns of a hill, valley, spur and col (fictional heights)

alt: Demographic transition model: birth and death rates start high at about 38 per 1,000 in stage 1; the death rate falls first in stage 2 so the gap (natural increase) and population grow fast; in stage 3 the birth rate falls; in stage 4 both rates are low and population is high and stable; in stage 5 the birth rate dips below the death rate and population falls slowly.
caption: Figure: the five stages of the demographic transition model (shape only; values illustrative)

alt: Cross-section through a mature depression moving east: the steep cold front with towering cumulonimbus and heavy short downpours, the warm sector with low stratus and drizzle, and the gently sloping warm front with nimbostratus and steady rain over a wide belt, thinning to cirrus far ahead.
caption: Figure: cross-section of a mature depression with the cold front, warm sector and warm front

alt: Hillside cross-section of a drainage basin: rain (800 mm a year) is intercepted by trees, infiltrates the soil, runs as overland flow or throughflow, percolates to groundwater and reaches the river as channel flow, while 600 mm is lost to evaporation and transpiration, leaving 200 mm of discharge.
caption: Figure: stores and flows in a drainage basin (water balance of the fictional 800 mm basin)

alt: Four drainage patterns seen from above: dendritic (tree-like, tributaries join the main river at acute angles), trellis (parallel main streams with short tributaries joining at right angles), radial (rivers flow outwards from a central high point), and parallel (streams side by side down a uniform slope).
caption: Figure: dendritic, trellis, radial and parallel drainage patterns (rivers in blue)

alt: Cross-section of the Earth drawn to scale in radius (about 6,370 km): a very thin crust of 5 to 70 km, a mantle down to about 2,900 km, a liquid outer core from 2,900 to 5,100 km and a solid inner core from 5,100 km to the centre.
caption: Figure: the layers of the Earth and their depths

alt: Systems diagram of a smallholder maize and cattle farm: inputs (physical, human and economic) pass through processes (ploughing, planting, weeding, harvesting, herding) to outputs (crops, milk and meat, manure, income, waste), and feedback arrows return income, seed and manure to the inputs.
caption: Figure: a farm as a system of inputs, processes, outputs and feedback

alt: Four fault structures in cross-section: a normal fault where tension makes one block slip down, a reverse fault where compression pushes one block up and over the other, a rift valley where a central block sinks between two faults, and a block mountain (horst) where a central block stands high between two faults.
caption: Figure: normal fault, reverse fault, rift valley and block mountain

alt: Cross-section of folded rock layers showing an anticline (arch) and a syncline (trough) with their limbs and axes, and sketches of four fold types as compression increases: simple, asymmetrical, overfold and recumbent.
caption: Figure: parts of a fold and the main types of fold

alt: A sketch of a map of a school with its seven components numbered: 1 title, 2 frame, 3 key, 4 scale bar, 5 north arrow, 6 numbered grid lines, 7 source and date, so a reader can interpret the symbols, measure distance and find direction.
caption: Figure: the seven components of a good map, labelled on a map of a fictional school

alt: Right-angled triangle on a map grid between 312 458 and 336 476: the points are 2.4 km apart eastwards and 1.8 km apart northwards, so the straight-line distance is the square root of (2.4 squared plus 1.8 squared), which is 3.0 km.
caption: Figure: the straight distance from 312 458 to 336 476 by Pythagoras' theorem is 3.0 km

alt: Extract L grid with eastings 27 to 30 and northings 13 to 15: the school lies in the shaded square 2813 and, at 6 tenths east and 7 tenths north of that square's corner, has the six-figure reference 286 137 (easting first).
caption: Figure: four-figure reference 2813 and six-figure reference 286 137 for the school in Extract L

alt: Five side views of a headland being eroded: waves widen a crack in the rock, which becomes a cave, then the cave cuts through to form an arch, the roof of the arch collapses leaving an isolated stack, and the stack is later undercut to a low stump.
caption: Figure: crack, cave, arch, stack and stump on an eroding headland

alt: Cross-section from a lookout tower at 1300 m to a dip tank at 1250 m over 2.5 km: the line of sight falls 20 m per km and is at 1270 m at 1.5 km, but a ridge there is 1320 m high, so the two places are not intervisible.
caption: Figure: a 1320 m ridge rises above the line of sight, so the dip tank cannot be seen from the tower

alt: Two stages of kopje formation: first, water rots granite along joints below the ground, leaving rounded corestones inside a thick layer of regolith; second, rain and rivers strip the regolith away, lowering the surface and leaving the corestones standing as a pile of boulders called a kopje.
caption: Figure: how a granite kopje forms by weathering along joints and then stripping of the regolith

alt: A meander in plan view with the fast, deep outside of the bend eroding a steep river cliff and the slow, shallow inside depositing a gentle slip-off slope, and a cross-section A to B across the bend showing the asymmetrical channel: steep cliff and deep water on one side, gentle slope and shallow water on the other.
caption: Figure: a meander in plan view and the asymmetrical cross-section A to B

alt: Four plan views of oxbow lake formation: erosion on the outer banks narrows the neck between two bends; in a flood the river cuts through the neck; deposition seals the old bend off from the new straight channel; the abandoned bend becomes a horseshoe-shaped oxbow lake.
caption: Figure: four stages in the formation of an oxbow lake

alt: Pie chart of employment in a fictional town: agriculture 45% is a sector of 162°, industry 20% is 72° and services 35% is 126°, which add up to 360°.
caption: Figure: sector angles of a pie chart are the percentage multiplied by 3.6

alt: Four plate boundaries: at a constructive boundary plates move apart and magma rises to make new crust; at a destructive boundary a dense oceanic plate is subducted under a continental plate forming a trench and volcanoes; at a collision boundary two continents crumple into fold mountains; at a conservative boundary plates slide past each other with earthquakes but no volcanoes.
caption: Figure: constructive, destructive, collision and conservative plate boundaries

alt: Two population pyramids on the same scale: a youthful pyramid (Zimbabwe-type) with a very wide base, about 40% aged under 15 and only about 3% aged 65 and over, and an ageing pyramid (Germany-type) with a narrow base, a bulge in middle age and about 21% aged 65 and over.
caption: Figure: a youthful and an ageing population pyramid (illustrative shapes)

alt: Scatter graph (fictional survey): land value falls from about US$900 per square metre at 0.5 km from the CBD to about US$100 at 5 km, a negative correlation shown by the dashed line of best fit; one site at 3 km is an anomaly at US$600.
caption: Figure: a scatter graph with a negative correlation, a line of best fit and one anomaly

alt: Schematic map extract of rural Zimbabwe: homesteads are scattered singly on the plateau in the north, clustered around a borehole, school and clinic in the centre, strung along a gravel road on a ridge in the south, with none on the river floodplain; the road from the village to the main road junction measures 4.6 cm.
caption: Figure: schematic map extract showing dispersed, nucleated and linear homesteads (fictional)

alt: Grid of nine squares (eastings 41 to 43, northings 64 to 66) with a hut in most squares: 14 huts packed around a borehole in square 4165 (nucleated), 9 huts along a road in square 4264 (linear), and single scattered huts elsewhere (dispersed). Total 30 huts.
caption: Figure: nucleated, linear and dispersed patterns on a fictional map grid

alt: Soil profile with six horizons from the surface down: O organic layer, A dark humus-rich topsoil, E pale eluviated layer from which minerals are washed out, B subsoil where minerals are washed in (illuviation), C weathered parent material and R solid bedrock.
caption: Figure: the horizons of a soil profile, O at the surface to R at the base

alt: Plan view of a spit: longshore drift carries sand along the coast in the direction of the prevailing wind; where the coastline changes direction the sand is deposited in calmer water and builds a ridge out into the sea, curving at the end, with a salt marsh developing in the sheltered water behind.
caption: Figure: a spit with longshore drift, a recurved end and a salt marsh behind

alt: Storm hydrograph from the lesson's example: rainfall peaks at 10:00, discharge rises from a base flow of 3 m³/s to a peak of 18 m³/s at 22:00 (a lag time of 12 hours, a rise of 15 m³/s) and then falls back along the falling limb.
caption: Figure: a storm hydrograph with base flow, rising limb, peak discharge, falling limb and lag time

alt: Two layouts for a sugar mill, with the same long distance to the market: beside the cane fields only 1 tonne of sugar makes the long journey, but with the mill in Harare all 10 tonnes of cane (the weight lost in processing) must travel, so weight-losing industries locate near their raw materials. Figures are approximate and the distance is illustrative.
caption: Figure: the weight-loss idea, about 10 t of cane makes about 1 t of sugar (approximate)

alt: Three urban land-use models: in the concentric model the CBD is at the centre and industry, then low-, medium- and high-income housing lie in rings further out; in the sector model zones run outwards in wedges, with industry and low-income housing in one sector and high-income housing in another; in the multiple-nuclei model several centres grow round separate nuclei.
caption: Figure: the concentric, sector and multiple-nuclei models of a town

alt: A V-shaped valley in cross-section, with steep straight sides and a narrow floor cut by vertical erosion, and in plan view where a small river winds between ridges (interlocking spurs) that project alternately from each side.
caption: Figure: a V-shaped valley in cross-section and interlocking spurs in plan view

alt: Cross-sections of two volcano types: a steep strato-volcano built of alternating layers of ash and lava, with a magma chamber, main vent, crater, side vent, lava flow and ash cloud (viscous magma, explosive eruptions), and a wide, gently sloping shield volcano built of runny basalt lava (gentle eruptions).
caption: Figure: a strato-volcano and a shield volcano in cross-section

alt: Long section of a waterfall: a hard rock cap lies over softer rock; the soft rock is eroded faster, a plunge pool is scoured and the hard rock overhangs, then collapses, so the falls retreat upstream and leave a gorge downstream.
caption: Figure: how a waterfall forms, retreats and leaves a gorge
